titre: Gulliver's Travels: The 1726 Text Is Not Swift's
accroche: In 1726, the publisher Motte cuts and alters Swift out of fear of prosecution. The text is largely restored in 1735, by Faulkner.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 28, 1726, two volumes published anonymously reach the bookshops of London, at a price of 8 shillings and 6 pence: *Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World*, by one Lemuel Gulliver. The book is an immediate success. But the text that readers hold in their hands is not quite Jonathan Swift's.

## A Manuscript Delivered in Secret

Swift finishes the work in 1725. The book is a satire plainly aimed at the Whigs, and it is likely that Swift had the manuscript copied out so that it could not be used as evidence against him, as in the affair of his Irish pamphlets. In March 1726, he comes to London, and the manuscript is handed over in secret to the printer Benjamin Motte, who divides the work among five print shops to go fast and avoid piracy.

Motte sees a best seller, but fears prosecution. He cuts or alters the riskiest passages, such as the contests at the court of Lilliput and the revolt of Lindalino, and adds to the second voyage a eulogy of Queen Anne.

## Gulliver's Reply

Swift protests behind a mask. In 1735, the Irish publisher George Faulkner publishes his works, and volume III gives the *Travels* with a new piece: a “Letter from Captain Gulliver to his Cousin Sympson,” dated 1727. Under the cousin's name, it is the publisher who is targeted.

Gulliver writes there that he does not remember authorizing that anything be deleted, still less that anything be added, and he disavows the paragraph on Queen Anne, who governed, he says, through chief ministers, Godolphin and then Oxford. As for the passages on the academy of projectors and the discourse to his Houyhnhnm master, they have been, he writes, omitted or changed to the point that he hardly knows his own work.

## A Reconstructed Text

Faulkner says he had access to a copy of Motte's edition annotated by a friend of the author, believed to be Charles Ford, which restored almost the whole manuscript. The original manuscript had been destroyed. The 1735 edition is generally regarded as the reference edition.

It is nonetheless not complete: the Lindalino episode, five paragraphs on a city's revolt against the flying island of Laputa, is missing from it too. It is reinstated only in 1899, in a new edition of the works, and modern editions add it to the Faulkner base.

What we read as Swift is therefore a reconstruction from a printed and annotated book, with no manuscript to check it against. What remains to be known is what the annotated copy did not say.

carte.punch: The 1726 Gulliver is cut by its publisher. Swift's text largely returns in 1735.
carte.idee: In 1726, Benjamin Motte, fearing prosecution, cuts and alters passages of Gulliver's Travels. Swift complains in 1735 through Gulliver's voice: “I do hardly know my own work.” With the manuscript destroyed, the text is reconstructed from an annotated copy.

quiz.question: What is the text restored by Faulkner in 1735 based on?
choix: Swift's autograph manuscript, kept in Dublin
A copy of Motte's edition annotated by a friend of Swift
Motte's corrected proofs, found at one of his printers
The French translation by the abbé Desfontaines, published as early as 1727
quiz.explication: The original manuscript had been destroyed: Faulkner relies on a copy of Motte's edition annotated by a friend of the author, probably Charles Ford. Neither an autograph in Dublin, nor recovered proofs, nor a French translation served as the basis of this edition.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Motte divide the manuscript among five print shops in 1726?
choix: To guarantee the author's anonymity with each printer
To go faster and avoid piracy
Because no London print shop had the necessary presses
On Swift's orders, since he feared a royal seizure
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says that Motte divides the work among five print shops to go fast and avoid piracy, not to protect anonymity or for lack of presses.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What addition does Motte make to the second voyage, absent from Swift's writing?
choix: A preface signed with his own name
A dedication to King George I
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Motte adds to the second voyage a eulogy of Queen Anne, which Gulliver will later disavow in his letter to Sympson.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what form does Swift make his disagreement with Motte's text known?
choix: A letter from Captain Gulliver to his cousin Sympson, published in 1735
A preface signed with his own name in the 1735 edition
An open letter published in a Dublin newspaper
A note added by Faulkner in his own name
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is through the voice of Captain Gulliver, in a letter addressed to his cousin Sympson dated 1727, that Swift voices his protest.
